hook.text: People have been kicking balls around for more than 2,000 years.

points.text: In ancient China, a game called cuju had players kick a ball through a net.
FIFA recognizes cuju as the earliest known form of football.
In medieval England, whole villages played rough 'mob football' with almost no rules.
In 1863, the Football Association was formed in London and wrote the first official rules.
Those rules split football from rugby: no carrying the ball with your hands.
FIFA, the world governing body, was founded in Paris in 1904.
The first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it.
Today football is the most popular sport on Earth, followed by billions of fans.

title: Safe Sleep Tips Every New Parent Should Know

hook.text: Newborns sleep up to 17 hours a day. Here's how to keep that sleep safe.

points.text: Newborns usually sleep 14 to 17 hours a day, in short stretches.
Always place babies on their back to sleep, for naps and at night.
Use a firm, flat mattress with just a fitted sheet.
Keep pillows, blankets, bumpers and soft toys out of the crib.
Experts recommend sharing a room, but not the same bed, for at least the first 6 months.
Dress the baby in light layers so they don't overheat.
A smoke-free home also lowers the risk of sleep-related problems.
Ask your pediatrician if you have any questions about your baby's sleep.

sources: American Academy of Pediatrics: Safe Sleep recommendations

title: Football Facts Even Fans Don't Know

hook.text: A pro footballer runs around 10 kilometers in a single match.

points.text: Midfielders often run the most, sometimes more than 11 kilometers a game.
A match lasts 90 minutes, split into two halves of 45.
The penalty spot is 11 meters, or 12 yards, from the goal line.
Goalkeepers are the only players who can use their hands, and only inside their own box.
A standard match ball measures about 68 to 70 centimeters around.
Pelé is credited with more than 1,000 goals, counting friendly matches.
During hard sprints, a young player's heart can beat more than 180 times a minute.
And yes: in most of the world, 'football' means the game you play with your feet.

title: How Your Heart Works in 90 Seconds

hook.text: Your heart beats around 100,000 times a day without you ever thinking about it.

points.text: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist.
It has four rooms, called chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles.
The right side pumps blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen.
The left side pumps that fresh blood out to the rest of your body.
Valves inside work like one-way doors so blood never flows backward.
The 'lub-dub' sound you hear is those valves snapping shut.
A tiny natural pacemaker sends electrical signals to set the rhythm.
Regular exercise helps keep this amazing muscle strong.

title: Are You Brushing Your Teeth Right?

hook.text: Many people brush for well under the recommended two minutes.

points.text: Dentists recommend brushing twice a day for two minutes each time.
Use a toothpaste with fluoride, which helps protect against cavities.
Brush gently in small circles. Scrubbing hard can hurt your gums.
Don't forget the inside surfaces and your tongue.
Clean between your teeth once a day with floss or a small brush.
Replace your toothbrush every three to four months, or sooner if the bristles fray.
Sugary drinks and snacks between meals feed the germs that cause cavities.
Regular dental checkups catch problems early.

hook.text: Babies are born with skills they lose as they grow up.

points.text: A newborn has about 300 bones. Many fuse together as they grow.
Newborns see best at about 20 to 30 centimeters, roughly the distance to a parent's face.
At first they see bold black-and-white patterns better than colors.
Put a finger in a newborn's palm and they'll grip it surprisingly tightly.
Hold a newborn upright with feet on a surface, and they'll make little stepping movements.
Babies' kneecaps start out as soft cartilage and turn to bone over the first few years.
Many newborns cry without tears for the first few weeks.
A newborn's head is about a quarter of its whole body length.
